1:1.headline: A "burden" on Nineveh: the Targum makes it a cup of curse
1:1.body: משא means a load, and also a prophecy that God "lifts" against a place. Ibn Ezra reads it that way, while Targum Jonathan, quoted by Rashi, makes it the weight of a cup of curse that Nineveh must drink.

sources.quote: משא - נבואה מה שנשא השם על נינוה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says משא is a prophecy that God lifted against Nineveh.

sources.quote: מְטַל כַּס דִלְוָט לְאַשְׁקָאָה יַת נִינְוֵה
sources.says: The Targum renders it "the weight of the cup of curse, to make Nineveh drink".

sources.quote: המשא מה שיספר דבר שקרה במשל ומליצה
sources.says: Malbim says a משא tells of something that happened, in parable and figure of speech.

1:2.headline: God "keeps" anger: stored up, not yet acted on
1:2.body: נטר means to keep or guard. Radak and Metzudat Zion say it means keeping a grudge, as in "do not bear a grudge", and Malbim says it is anger held in the heart, while vengeance is anger acted out.

sources.quote: ונוטר. כמו שומר ר"ל אף על פי שאינו לוקח נקמתו מאויביו מיד שומר הוא העון להם
sources.says: Radak says it means "keeps": even if God does not take revenge at once, He keeps the sin for them.

sources.quote: ונוטר. ענין שמירת איבה כמו לא תקום ולא תטור
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means keeping hatred, as in "do not take revenge and do not bear a grudge".

sources.quote: ויש הבדל בין נוקם ובין נוטר שהנטירה היא בלב והנקימה הוא בפועל
sources.says: Malbim says keeping a grudge is in the heart, while taking revenge is in action.

1:2.headline: Who are God's "enemies"? Maimonides says only idol worshippers
1:2.body: Maimonides says that in the whole Bible, only an idol worshipper is called God's enemy or foe, and he quotes this verse. Malbim tells the two words apart: a foe does harm, an enemy only wishes it.

sources.quote: ולא תמצא שנקרא "אויב ה'" או "צר" או "שונא" אלא עובד עבודה זרה דווקא
sources.says: Maimonides says you will find no one called God's enemy, foe or hater except an idol worshipper.

sources.quote: שהצר מציר בפועל,והאויב דורש רעה בלב ואינו מציר בפועל
sources.says: Malbim says a foe does harm in action, while an enemy wishes harm in his heart but does not act.

1:3.headline: Great in power: strong enough to hold back His anger
1:3.body: Why put "slow to anger" next to "great in power"? Radak, Ibn Ezra and Malbim say real strength is the power to hold back, as Moses prayed "let the power of God be great" just before "slow to anger".

sources.quote: גדול כח הוא לסבול כעסו שלא ינקם מיד וכן אמר משה רבינו עליו השלום יגדל נא כח ה'
sources.says: Radak says God has great power to bear His anger and not take revenge at once, as Moses said, "let the power of God be great".

sources.quote: משל לאדם שיש לו כח גדול אז ימשול בכעסו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like a person of great strength, who can rule his anger.

sources.quote: כי בשר ודם אי אפשר לו להאריך אפו מצד קוצר כחו לסבול
sources.says: Malbim says a human being cannot hold back anger long, because his strength to bear it is short.

1:3.headline: The clouds are the dust kicked up by His feet
1:3.body: The verse pictures clouds as the dust under God's feet. Malbim says it is as if He runs and raises dust, and Radak says the dust stands for the darkness His decrees bring on His enemies.

sources.quote: והוא אבק רגליו כאילו בהליכתו במרוצה מעלה אבק והוא הענן
sources.says: Malbim says it is as if, running, He kicks up dust, and that dust is the cloud.

sources.quote: אבק רגליו הגזרות הבאות מסבתו על האויבים הם להם לחושך ואפלה והמשילם לאבק הנופל מתחת הרגלים
sources.says: Radak says the decrees He brings on His enemies are darkness for them, and the verse compares them to dust falling under the feet.

sources.quote: וענן אבק רגליו - דרך משל למרוצת העננים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a picture of clouds racing along.

1:4.headline: Lebanon's blossom: the sages saw the Temple's golden trees
1:4.body: Plainly the flowers of Lebanon wither. Rashi brings the sages, who read it as the golden fruit trees Solomon planted in the Temple, which withered when the nations entered.

sources.quote: חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל פֵּרְשׁוּ כְּלַפֵּי מִינֵי מְגָדִים שֶׁנָּטַע שְׁלֹמֹה בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ שֶׁהָיוּ שֶׁל זָהָב, וְכֵיוָן שֶׁנִּכְנְסוּ גּוֹיִם לַהֵיכָל יָבְשׁוּ
sources.says: Rashi says the sages explained it as the golden fruit trees Solomon planted in the Temple, which dried up when the nations entered the sanctuary.

sources.quote: וכן פרחי עצי הלבנון ייבשו
sources.says: Radak reads it plainly: the blossoms of Lebanon's trees dry up.

1:8.headline: A flood of anger, or the real flood that broke Nineveh?
1:8.body: Rashi reads "a passing flood" as God's sweeping wrath. Malbim reads it as the real flood of the Tigris, which he says swept into Nineveh at God's command.

sources.quote: וּבְשֶׁטֶף עֹבֵר. וּבְחֵמָה שׁוֹטֶפֶת
sources.says: Rashi says it means with sweeping wrath.

sources.quote: והוא ציור על זרם מי חדקל ששטף אז נינוה בפקודת ה'
sources.says: Malbim says it pictures the waters of the Tigris that flooded Nineveh then at God's command.

sources.quote: האויב הבא והוא נ״נ הוא יכלה הכל כמו שטף מים העובר
sources.says: Metzudat David says the coming enemy, Nebuchadnezzar, will destroy everything like a rushing flood.

1:11.headline: Beliya'al: one who throws off the yoke of heaven
1:11.body: בליעל is a common word for a wicked person. Metzudat Zion reads it as בלי עול, "without a yoke": someone who has thrown off the yoke of heaven.

sources.quote: בליעל. בלי עול שמים ר״ל רשע
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בליעל means "without the yoke of heaven", that is, wicked.

sources.quote: והוא יועץ עצת בליעל לפרוק עול ולעשות כל התועבות
sources.says: Malbim says he gave worthless counsel, to throw off the yoke and do every abomination.

1:14.headline: "You are worthless", or "you are burned"?
1:14.body: קלות usually means made light, despised. Malbim adds a second reading, burned in fire, as in "whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire".

sources.quote: כי קלות. מענין בזיון, ויל"פ קלות, נשרפת באש, מענין אשר קלם מלך בבל באש
sources.says: Malbim says it means disgrace, and it can also mean "you were burned in fire", as in "whom the king of Babylon roasted in fire".

sources.quote: היית נקלה ונבזה כי בניך יהרגוך ועוד בבית אלהיך
sources.says: Radak says you were made worthless and despised, since your sons will kill you, and in your god's house.

sources.quote: כִּי קַלּוֹתָ. בְּעֵינַי
sources.says: Rashi says it means "you were light in My eyes".

2:3.headline: God restored Jacob's pride, or let it rest
2:3.body: שב usually means returned or restored. Metzudat Zion reads it as rest, as in בשובה ונחת, 'in stillness and quiet'. Radak brings both views from the early grammarians.

sources.quote: ענין השקט ומרגוע כמו בשובה ונחת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means quiet and rest.

sources.quote: ואם כדברי ר' יהודה יהיה ענין הנחה והשקט
sources.says: Radak says by Rabbi Yonah it means 'restored', and by Rabbi Judah it means rest and quiet.

2:3.headline: Stripped like a vine
2:3.body: בקק means to empty out. Rashi and Malbim say the word is used for a vine stripped of its grapes. That fits the next words, which speak of the ruined vine branches.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ׳בְּקִיקָה׳ נוֹפֵל עַל גֶּפֶן
sources.says: Rashi says it means plundered and emptied, a word used for a vine.

sources.quote: בא תמיד על הרקת פרי הגפן
sources.says: Malbim says the word is always used for stripping the fruit of a vine.

2:4.headline: Cypress spears dipped in poison, or men wrapped, or trembling
2:4.body: הרעלו is read three ways. Rashi says wrapped, like a veil. Radak says spears of cypress wood dipped in poison. His father said the 'cypresses' are Nineveh's nobles, and they trembled.

sources.quote: מְעֻטָּפִין, וְדוֹמֶה לוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means wrapped, like the veils in Isaiah 3.

sources.quote: מן תרעלה שמפרשים סם המות, ואדוני אבי ז"ל פי' תרעלה רעדה
sources.says: Radak says it comes from poison, and his father read it as trembling.

2:6.headline: Running to the wall, or to her wall
2:6.body: The ה at the end can mean two things. Rashi says it means 'to', as if a ל stood at the start: they run to the wall. Radak says it means 'her': the wall of Nineveh.

sources.quote: כָּל תֵּיבָה הַצְּרִיכָה לָמֶ״ד בִּתְחִלָּתָהּ הִטִּיל לָהּ הֵ״א בְּסוֹפָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says any word that needs a ל at its start may take a ה at its end instead.

sources.quote: הה"א במפיק ר"ל חומת נינוה
sources.says: Radak says the ה is sounded and means 'her', the wall of Nineveh.

2:6.headline: A siege shield, or the king who shields
2:6.body: סוכך means something that covers. Radak says it is a roof of planks and hides that sappers work under at the wall. Rashi also offers 'the king', as in the 'covering cherub', a word for a ruler.

sources.quote: הוא מכסה קרשים ועורות עליהם
sources.says: Radak says it is a cover of planks and hides that attackers go under to dig at the wall.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ ״מִמְשַׁח הַסּוֹכֵךְ״, לְשׁוֹן ׳מוֹשֵׁל׳
sources.says: Rashi says it may mean the king arming himself, since סוכך can mean a ruler.

2:10.headline: Glory, or a city swept clean
2:10.body: כבד usually means weight or glory. Rashi reads it as sweeping out, like מכבד הבית, sweeping a house: Nineveh is swept bare of every treasure. Metzudat Zion gives both readings.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ׳מְכַבֵּד הַבַּיִת׳
sources.says: Rashi says it means sweeping, as one sweeps a house, so the city is swept of its treasures.

sources.quote: מל׳ כבוד או הוא ענין טיאוט וגריפה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means glory, or else sweeping and scraping out.

2:11.headline: Empty, emptied, laid waste: three words that echo
2:11.body: The verse opens with three words that sound alike: בוקה ומבוקה ומבלקה. The commentators say the repeat makes the point stronger. Malbim says the added מ makes the emptiness even greater.

sources.quote: ענין ריקות והכפל לחזק
sources.says: Radak says the words mean emptiness and are doubled for strength.

sources.quote: תוספת המ"ם מורה על הגדלת הריקות
sources.says: Malbim says the added מ shows the emptiness growing.

2:11.headline: Faces black as a cooking pot
2:11.body: פארור is rare. Metzudat Zion says it is a pot, as in the manna that was cooked בפרור. Rashi says the faces turned black like the soot on a pot.

sources.quote: שַׁחְרוּרִית כַּקְּדֵרָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means blackness like a pot.

sources.quote: קדרה כמו ובשלו בפרור
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a pot, as in the cooking of the manna.

3:1.headline: פרק means plunder: something torn out of its owner's hand
3:1.body: This is a rare word. Rashi and Radak both read it as robbery, taking a thing by pulling it loose from someone else's hand.

sources.quote: גֶּזֶל שֶׁמְּפָרְקוֹ מִיַּד בְּעָלָיו
sources.says: Rashi says פרק is theft: a thing pulled away from its owner's hand.

sources.quote: והוא כמו גזל שפורק דבר מיד אחר וכן ופרקת עולו
sources.says: Radak says it is like robbery, which takes a thing out of another's hand, and compares ופרקת עולו (you will break his yoke).

3:3.headline: כבד: a heavy pile of dead, or sweeping them up?
3:3.body: Radak says כבד means a great number, so the verse says "many slain" and "heaps of bodies" in two ways. Malbim says it is a word for sweeping, found in the language of the Mishnah.

sources.quote: כמו רב חלל ענין כפל במלות שונות כי כבד הוא ענין רבוי
sources.says: Radak says the verse repeats itself in different words, because כבד means abundance.

sources.quote: טאטוא בלשון המשנה
sources.says: Malbim says this word means sweeping, in the language of the Mishnah.

3:8.headline: חיל here means a low wall in front of the main wall
3:8.body: Metzudat Zion says חיל means the low wall in front of the high one. Rashi says the sea served the city as both חיל and wall, and gives the Aramaic שורא ובר שורא.

sources.quote: הוא החומה הנמוכה שלפני הגבוה וכן ויאבל חיל וחומה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חיל is the low wall before the high one, as in ויאבל חיל וחומה.

sources.quote: אֲשֶׁר הָיָה הַיָּם לָהּ לְחַיִל וּלְחוֹמָה, שׁוּרָא וּבַר שׁוּרָא
sources.says: Rashi says the sea was both חיל and wall for the city, in the Aramaic terms שורא ובר שורא.

3:10.headline: Exile and captivity: one idea twice, or two different fates?
3:10.body: The verse says the city went into גולה and into שבי. Radak says the verse says it twice to strengthen the point. Malbim says they differ, because a person in exile may be free to go where he likes.

sources.quote: ואמר בגולה ואמר בשבי כפל הענין במ"ש לחזק הענין
sources.says: Radak says the verse says "in exile" and "in captivity" as a repeat, to strengthen the point.

sources.quote: כי יש גולה שאינו שבוי רק יכול ללכת בכ"מ שירצה
sources.says: Malbim says there is an exile who is not a captive and can go anywhere he wishes.

3:10.headline: רתקו means bound in chains, from a word in Isaiah and Ezekiel
3:10.body: This is a rare verb. Rashi reads it from רתקות כסף and הרתוק, words for chains. Radak adds that בזקים (chains) is only extra explanation, since רתקו alone would do.

sources.quote: נִכְבְּלוּ, לְשׁוֹן ״רְתֻקוֹת כֶּסֶף״ (ישעיהו מ:יט), ״עֲשֵׂה הָרַתּוֹק״ (יחזקאל ז:כג), שַׁלְשְׁלָאוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it means they were bound, from רתקות כסף in Isaiah and הרתוק in Ezekiel: chains.

sources.quote: הוא תוספת ביאור כי די לו ברתקו
sources.says: Radak says adding בזיקים is extra explanation, since רתקו would have been enough.

3:14.headline: מלבן: a brick mold, a brick kiln, or a brickyard?
3:14.body: This is a rare word. Rashi says it is the mold used to shape bricks. Radak says it is the kiln where bricks are burned. Ibn Ezra says it is the place where bricks are made.

sources.quote: הַמַּלְבֵּן הֶעָשׂוּי לִדְפוּס הַלְּבֵנִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is the מלבן made as the mold of the bricks.

sources.quote: כמו כבשן הלבנים ששורפים אותם בו
sources.says: Radak says it is like a brick kiln, where bricks are burned.

sources.quote: מקום מעשה הלבנים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the place where bricks are made.

3:15.headline: התכבד can mean "be swept away" or "become a great crowd"
3:15.body: Rashi first reads it as being swept with brooms of destruction. He adds that some read it as covering yourself with a heavy mass of troops, like locusts.

sources.quote: בְּמַטְאֲטֵי הַשְׁמֵד
sources.says: Rashi says it means being swept with brooms of destruction.

sources.quote: וְיֵשׁ פּוֹתְרִין ״הִתְכַּבֵּד כַּיֶּלֶק״ – תִּתְכַּסִּי בְּכֹבֶד גְּיָסוֹת כְּיֶלֶק
sources.says: Rashi says some explain it as covering yourself with a heavy mass of troops, like a locust.

sources.quote: וי"מ התכבד המכבדי מדברי רז"ל מכבדין בין המטות
sources.says: Radak says some read it as "sweeping", from the sages' word for sweeping between the beds.

3:16.headline: פשט: spread out over the land, or strip off a skin?
3:16.body: Radak reads the locust spreading over the land and then flying off. Malbim reads it as the locust shedding its covering, like ופשט את בגדיו (and he took off his clothes), and then flying.

sources.quote: כמו הילק שפשט בארץ ואחר כך עף קל מהרה
sources.says: Radak says it is like the locust that spread over the land and then quickly flew off.

sources.quote: כמו ופשט את בגדיו
sources.says: Malbim says it is like ופשט את בגדיו, the locust taking off its earlier body and covering.

3:17.headline: כגוב גובי: the biggest kind of locust, like "king of kings"
3:17.body: Both words are rare names for locusts. Radak says the doubled form means the biggest kind of locust, as in מלך מלכים (king of kings). Ibn Ezra says it works like קדש קדשים (holy of holies).

sources.quote: ר"ל המין הגדול שבמיני הארבה כמו מלך מלכים
sources.says: Radak says it means the largest of the kinds of locust, like king of kings.

sources.quote: כגוב גובי - כמו יוצר גובי. כמו קדש קדשים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says כגוב גובי is like יוצר גובי, and like קדש קדשים.

3:18.headline: נפשו: scattered, or resting? Two opposite readings
3:18.body: Rashi says it means scattered, the same as נפוצו, because ש and צ can swap places. Metzudat Zion says it comes from נופש (rest), as in שבת וינפש.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ ׳נָפֹצוּ׳, וְכָל הָאוֹתִיּוֹת הַיּוֹצֵאת מִמּוֹצָא אֶחָד מִתְחַלְּפוֹת זוֹ בָּזוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is like נפצו, since letters from the same place in the mouth swap with each other.

sources.quote: הוא מל׳ נופש ומרגוע כמו שבת וינפש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is from the word for rest and ease, as in שבת וינפש.

3:19.headline: תקעו כף: clap for joy, or shake hands against you?
3:19.body: Radak reads it as clapping hands for joy at her fall. Malbim allows a second reading: they sealed a pact by striking hands, to fight against her.

sources.quote: עליה לשמחה, כמו ויכו כף ויאמרו יחי המלך
sources.says: Radak says it is about her, for joy, like "they clapped hands and said, long live the king".

sources.quote: או רצה לומר שהתחברו בתקיעת כף נגדך להלחם אתך
sources.says: Malbim says it may mean they joined by striking hands against you, to fight you.
